name: Brazilian / intimate waxing

lead: Intimate waxing leaves the area smooth and hair-free for several weeks, in styles from a swimsuit-line trim (American) through a landing strip (French) to full removal (Brazilian or Hollywood). The result is visible immediately. The name is traced to a Manhattan salon founded in 1987.

Wax grips the hair and pulls it out from the follicle, so regrowth typically takes around four to six weeks. Proponents say repeated waxing can weaken regrowth and make sessions less painful and less frequent. A 2016 JAMA Dermatology survey of 3,316 US women found 84% reported lifetime pubic hair grooming; male waxing has become more common.

paras: Done in a salon with warm or cold wax and cloth strips, or stripless hard wax, and repeated every few weeks as hair returns.

Pain varies from slight to severe. Bumps and ingrown hairs can last two to five days, and folliculitis has been reported to be rising among women who wax or shave the bikini area. People with weakened immune systems face higher infection risk if waxing is done improperly, and skin lifting is more likely with certain medications.

chain: Wax pulls hair from the root
angle.text: Wax pulls pubic hair out from the root, from a swimsuit-line trim to full removal, leaving smooth skin for several weeks. The result is visible immediately and the practice is well documented.

lead: Brazilian waxing, also called intimate or bikini waxing, is the removal of pubic hair with hot or cold wax, lifted off with cloth strips or, in stripless forms, peeled away once hardened.[1][2] People use it to get a smooth, hair-free finish around the bikini line or swimwear area that lasts for weeks rather than days, and some choose it for how clean, sleek or youthful the result looks.[1] Styles range from the American, which removes only the hair a swimsuit would show, through the French, which leaves a narrow vertical strip, to the Brazilian or Hollywood, which removes all or nearly all hair.[1]

The Brazilian name is credited to the J. Sisters salon in Manhattan, opened in 1987 by seven sisters from Brazil.[1] Waxing is mainly associated with women, though male waxing has become more common.[1] Prevalence data come from surveys: a 2016 JAMA Dermatology study of 3,316 American women reported that 84% had groomed pubic hair at some point, with hygiene the most-cited reason.[1]
Reported downsides include pain, bumps, ingrown hairs and folliculitis.[1][2] No clinical trial has tested Brazilian waxing as an intervention; the evidence is survey and descriptive material.

paras: In a typical session the area is cleaned with an antiseptic and powdered, wax is applied in the direction of hair growth in strips, and removed against it while the skin is held taut. Long hair may be trimmed first, and a patch test on the upper thigh is commonly recommended to check for allergy.[1] Bikini wax is often a beeswax and tall oil blend, described as stronger on coarse pubic hair than the synthetic waxes used on legs.[1]

Soft or strip wax is spread thinly and removed with a cloth strip, while hard or film wax is applied thicker and peeled off without a strip; hard wax is described as suited to sensitive skin and potentially less painful.[2] Ibuprofen taken beforehand and topical anaesthetics are mentioned as ways to reduce pain, and growth-inhibiting products are sometimes applied afterwards to slow regrowth.[1]

The American or basic bikini wax removes hair outside a swimsuit triangle and typically takes 20 to 30 minutes. The French wax leaves a landing strip roughly 3.8 cm wide and 7.6 cm long, and is sometimes called a partial Brazilian. The full Brazilian removes hair from the whole area, sometimes leaving a thin strip, and salons use names such as Hollywood or Full Monty.[1]

Pubic hair removal has been recorded in several cultures: an ethnologist in 1901 observed it as a custom of Nair women in India, and in Islam removal of unwanted body hair is regarded as part of fitra, or natural practice.[1] The introduction of the bikini in 1946, reduced swimwear coverage and changes in lingerie are linked to greater interest in grooming.[1]

Some people regard a fully bare result as glamorous or youthful-looking, while others style or skip grooming for identity or cost reasons.[1] Critics argue the Brazilian can make adult women look underage and may account for its popularity in the sex industry; this is a recorded criticism of the style.[1] Bikini waxing has also been credited with a decline in pubic lice cases.[1]

Pain ranges from slight to severe, may be greater during pregnancy and may lessen over later sessions.[1] Bumps and ingrown hairs occur, with discomfort typically lasting two to five days; isolated ingrown hairs can be removed with tweezers or electrolysis.[1] Medical providers have reported an increase in folliculitis among women who wax or shave the bikini area, and people with weakened immune systems face a higher infection risk if waxing is done improperly.[1]

Skin lifting is more likely with blood thinners, steroids, autoimmune drugs, topical retinoids, recent sunburn, laser or peels, and conditions such as eczema or psoriasis. Waxing can also trigger cold sores in people with a history of them.[2]

No studies found testing Brazilian waxing as an intervention. A 2016 survey in JAMA Dermatology of 3,316 US women described how common grooming is (84% lifetime) and why women do it, without evaluating waxing outcomes.[1]
